opus-5.5.text:
I think the boundary between pretraining and post-training is much blurrier than the org chart usually suggests. If you split them into two separate teams, each with its own metrics and its own sense of ownership, you end up optimizing locally. The pretraining team chases benchmark numbers on the base model, the post-training team inherits whatever they get and tries to patch it up, and nobody is really responsible for the final capability of the model as a whole.

In practice, a lot of the most important questions sit right on that boundary. What data mixture should go into the late stage of pretraining so the model is easier to align afterward? How much reasoning-style data do you put in mid-training versus leave for RL? When the RL stage hits a ceiling, is that a post-training problem, or is the base model simply missing some knowledge or ability? You can only answer these well if the same people can see both sides and move freely between them.

So I prefer to organize around problems and goals rather than training stages. Someone might work on data for pretraining one month and on reward design the next, because that's where the bottleneck is. It also matters for culture. When people feel they own a stage, they tend to defend it. When they feel they own the model, they're more willing to say, "This doesn't belong in my part; it should be fixed upstream," or the opposite. That kind of honesty is what lets a relatively small team move fast.

And the field changes quickly. The techniques that define post-training today, especially large-scale RL, are pulling more and more compute and starting to look like a kind of continued pretraining. If your structure is frozen around last year's pipeline, you'll be slow to adapt. Keeping things fluid is a way of staying open to how the recipe itself evolves.

r001.rationale: The response argues that fixed divisions encourage local optimization and slow adaptation, but it does not state that they stifle researchers’ creativity.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify a diversity perspective as an important requirement for post-training.

r003.rationale: It mentions data mixtures and training stages, but does not say that pretraining practitioners’ habitual attention to data diversity benefits post-training.

fable-5.1.text:
Because the boundary is artificial. Pretraining and post-training are not two products; they are two stages of shaping the same model, and most of the hard problems live exactly at the seam between them. If you draw a hard line and assign separate teams, each side optimizes its own metrics. The pretraining team pushes loss and benchmarks, the post-training team patches whatever comes out, and nobody owns the question of what the base model should actually be good at so that alignment and instruction-following become easy rather than a rescue operation.

I think of it as one continuous data and training pipeline. The data mix you choose in the middle and late stages of pretraining already determines how much headroom you have in SFT and RL. Conversely, what you learn from post-training, which capabilities are brittle and which behaviors the model resists, is the best signal you have for what to put back into pretraining data. If those two groups only meet at a handoff, that feedback loop runs once a cycle. If it is the same people, or at least people who rotate across both, it runs every week.

There is also a people reason. Researchers who only ever see one side develop blind spots. Someone who has only done post-training tends to overestimate how much can be fixed late. Someone who has only done pretraining tends to underestimate how much behavior is downstream of alignment choices. I want the team to hold the whole picture, so when we debate a decision, everyone is reasoning about the final model, not defending their stage. A small team can afford that fluidity, and I think it is actually one of the main advantages a small team has over a large lab with rigid org charts.

r002.rationale: It discusses differing perspectives across pretraining and post-training, but does not identify a diversity perspective as an important requirement for post-training.

r003.rationale: It mentions that the data mix affects later training, but does not say pretraining practitioners habitually attend to data diversity or that this is an advantage they bring to post-training.

astra-6.text:
I think of pretraining and post-training as parts of one continuous process. A problem that shows up during post-training may come from the pretraining data or objective. If the teams are separated too rigidly, it’s easy for each side to optimize its own metrics without improving the model as a whole.

I’d rather organize people around the problem we’re trying to solve. You still need specialization, but people should be able to follow a question across those boundaries, share findings, and change the approach together. The division of work should help the research, rather than determine what questions we’re allowed to ask.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the boundary between pretraining and post-training isn’t fixed technically, I don’t think we should make it rigid organizationally. Both contribute to the capability of the final model, and decisions in one stage affect what’s possible in the other.

If you divide the teams too sharply, people can end up optimizing their own stage rather than the final result. A problem that appears during post-training might be better solved by changing the pretraining data or objective. You want that feedback to travel easily, and you want people to be able to work across the boundary.

That doesn’t mean there’s no specialization. It means organizing around the problems we need to solve, while letting the division of work evolve with the technology.

r001.rationale: The response says rigid divisions can encourage stage-specific optimization and impede feedback, but it does not state that they stifle researchers’ creativity.
